Rain will continue overnight into Tuesday across northern Latvia, with prolonged and heavy rainfall expected in some areas. Localised heavy downpours and thunderstorms are also forecast. During the day, rain will spread across a much larger part of the country, while strong showers and thunderstorms may continue in some areas during the afternoon and into the night, particularly in central and eastern Latvia. Wednesday is also expected to be wet across much of the country, especially in the central and eastern regions. Fog may develop overnight and during the morning hours in some locations, reducing visibility. Northeasterly and northerly winds will gradually shift to northwesterly and westerly directions while remaining gusty. Along the Kurzeme coast, wind gusts are expected to reach 15–19 metres per second, and could briefly reach 20 metres per second early Tuesday. Night-time temperatures will range between +10°C and +15°C, while daytime temperatures will generally reach +15°C to +20°C. On Thursday and Friday, skies will remain mostly cloudy, although occasional sunny spells are expected. Scattered rain showers are possible, but winds will ease and remain light. Temperatures will stay similar to previous days, with much of the country seeing daytime highs of around +20°C on Friday. Over the weekend and at the beginning of next week, cyclonic conditions will continue to influence the region. Skies will remain mostly cloudy with occasional clear periods, while isolated rain showers are expected. Light winds will prevail. As warmer air gradually moves into Latvia from the south, temperatures will slowly rise. By Monday, daytime highs are expected to reach +20°C to +25°C across most of the country. Photograph: Ugo Amez/SIPA/Shutterstock France Schoolboy, 15, loses hand after picking up police stun grenade during French school protests PM orders ministers to tackle students’ five major demands, including organising replacement teachers and school repairs Europe live – latest updates Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.25 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of schools in France remained fully or partly closed on Monday as teenagers continued to blockade buildings and the government struggled to contain the biggest youth protest movement in years. A 15-year-old protesting against what the demonstrators say are France’s dilapidated ⁠and understaffed ​schools ‌had his hand ‌blown off on ‌Monday in the northern town of Lens, the local prefect François-Xavier Lauch ‌said. A local newspaper, La Voix du ​Nord, reported that the teenager lost his hand after ⁠picking up a ​police stun ​grenade. Lauch said ​an investigation ​into ‌the incident ​had ​been opened. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, had earlier attempted to calm the protests by accepting schoolchildren’s grievances as “legitimate” and saying the government must listen. Lecornu ordered ministers to tackle the students’ five major demands. These include organising the replacement of absent teachers, in recognition that pupils in some areas miss months of teaching because of staff absences – even in key exam years. Lecornu also called for a review of France’s lengthy school days, which are among the longest in Europe . The government will also look at repairs to dilapidated school buildings. Children on blockades across France have described water leaking into classrooms during class, cockroaches, collapsing ceilings and unbearable heat in summer . Lecornu said ministers must come up with proposals by the end of the month. Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT trade union, said the government was late in offering to tackle the schoolchildren’s demands. She said the number of absent teachers who were not replaced had doubled in 10 years and class sizes were at a record high. “Amid such anger, a few measures just for show aren’t going to satisfy demands,” Binet said. She called for the government to instead stop all budget cuts as well as cuts to teachers’ positions. Student unions have called for a national day of protest on Tuesday with more schools expected to be barricaded. Thousands of trade unionists, teachers, public sector workers and parents’ groups are expected to join marches of support in cities and towns across France. Binet said trade unionists would march to ensure there was no violence on the edge of any protests on Tuesday, as she criticised heavy policing. “We’ve been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students,” she said. University students continued to support the school protests on Monday, with up to 40 university buildings blockaded across France. Philippe Baptiste, the minister for higher education, told French radio he felt student and high school protests could intensify with the national protests on Tuesday. Between 400 and 500 high schools are expected to remain completely or partly closed on ⁠Monday out of a total of 3,700, the education minister said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion “Our priority is to restore order,” ‌the government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday. The protests began in late September ‌at a high school ‌in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages. The government was taken by surprise as protests then spread nationwide, amid anger at social inequality and a lack of investment in the education system. Since last Monday, about 5,000 people, mostly ‌teenagers, have been arrested across France and dozens injured. The family of a 16-year-old school pupil in Tours has filed a complaint for police violence after he lost sight in his right eye. The state prosecutor said the boy’s injuries were in line with the impact from a of police rubber bullet. A police investigation is under way. Teachers have also been injured. Damage to property is estimated in the tens ​of millions of euros. http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279322.text: An inconvenient truth: Why the EU could lose twice to Alisher Usmanov RT.com 22 Sep 2026, 02:31 GMT+10 The blocs case against the tycoon was built on sand and its media industry has had to amend thousands of articles The EU is divided over a deal to un-sanction Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov. Brussels' allies in Kiev aren't happy, but the alternative - a legal showdown - could call the bloc's entire sanctions regime into question. Ambassadors from EU member states met on Monday to discuss Usmanov's case. According to Euronews, France pushed for Usmanov's removal from the blacklist, in exchange for Azerbaijan freeing two alleged French spies. Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, proposed that Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, another Russian businessman, be delisted on the condition that the EU renew its anti-Russian sanctions regime for 36 months instead of the usual six. After a second round of talks on Monday that stretched into the night, EU envoys failed to agree to remove Usmanov and Fridman from the list. Meaning no agreement has been reached on extending the bloc's sanctions. Usmanov is at the centre of a discussion that could undo a central pillar of the EU's personal sanctions policy. Why was Usmanov sanctioned? Police raid Alisher Usmanov's Tegernsee lakeside villa in Rottach-Egern, Germany, September 21, 2022 Getty Images; Alexandra Beier A highly successful entrepreneur in the final years of the Soviet Union, the Russian-Uzbek businessman snapped up metal and mining businesses during the rapid privatization of the 1990s, breached into media with his acquisition of Russia's Kommersant newspaper in 2006, and expanded his wealth with a series of savvy investments in Apple, Twitter, and Facebook over the following decade. Usmanov, believed to be Russia's seventh-richest person with a net worth of more than $16 billion, was sanctioned by the EU four days after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. The EU's sanctions ledger declared that Usmanov "has particularly close ties to the President of the Russian Federation, Vladimir Putin," has "acted on behalf of the President of the Russian Federation in a number of business deals," and gave former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev "personal use of luxurious residences" controlled by his companies. Alisher Usmanov's entry in the EU's sanctions ledger, February 28, 2022 "Kommersant under Usmanov's ownership published a propagandist anti-Ukrainian article by Dmitry Medvedev" the entry continued, concluding that "therefore he actively supported the Russian government's policies of destabilization of Ukraine." EU media: Unreliable sources According to Usmanov's lawyers, Brussels sourced all of its "reasons and evidence" for sanctioning the billionaire from "mass media and social media publications." In a letter to the European Council last month seen by Intellinews journalist Ben Aris, Usmanov's legal team argued that this evidence has been proven false in courts in all 27 EU member states. Back in 2022, Usmanov launched a sweeping campaign of litigation against newspapers and other media outlets incorrectly reporting his business links to the Russian government and characterizing him as "Putin's favorite oligarch." Usmanov won judgments against Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), which claimed that he used his wealth "in the interests or at the direction of the Kremlin," against German state broadcaster ARD, which connected him to a "bribery scheme," and against Luxembourg's Mediahuis, which named him as the owner of a sanctioned superyacht impounded in Hamburg. Among his other legal victories were judgments against Forbes, Germany's Der Tagesspiegel, Austria's Kurier, and Switzerland's Blick, all of which used false claims by deceased anti-Kremlin activist Alexey Navalny to back up their stories of Usmanov's ties to the Kremlin. The European Council could stand accused Since 2022, his lawyers reportedly claimed in the letter, more than 3,200 articles about Usmanov have been corrected and 1,300 deleted, in 60 countries. Almost 100 cease-and-desist letters have been issued and 58,000 pieces of online content and ads about the businessman have been pulled down, many of which "relied on the Council's narrative." The European Council, meanwhile, has quietly removed at least 18 documents from its "evidence packs" against Usmanov, the letter claimed. The wave of retractions and deletions - issued by the same sources used to back up the sanctions decision - "must be accepted as exculpatory evidence," Usmanov's lawyers wrote. "To sum up, the allegations used to maintain Mr Usmanov's designation have been discredited and refuted in 27 out of 27 EU Member States." The EU's dilemma The EU's Court of Justice has already dismissed two attempts by Usmanov to appeal his blacklisting. In rejecting the second attempt last September, the court ruled that the council's decision to sanction Usmanov was based on a "specific, precise and consistent" body of evidence. However, even Politico, the Brussels elite's leak-factory of choice, has reported that the "evidence packs" used to justify sanctioning figures like Usmanov are often "hastily compiled" and based on "shaky evidence." In 2023, Politico found that evidence against Russian businessman Grigory Berezkin was drawn from articles written by an AI chatbot, and a website called 'Russian Crimes' written by journalists that didn't exist. Another evidence pack cited an advertisement in a Russian lifestyle and cooking magazine. Yet another cited a Ukrainian gossip site. Berezhkin was removed from the EU's blacklist that September. More than a dozen individuals have since been removed from the list. Some, like Formula 1 driver Nikita Mazepin, had been sanctioned over the alleged offenses of their relatives. At least six - including Pavel Ezubov, cousin of metals magnate Oleg Deripaska, and former e-commerce tycoon Aleksandr Shulgin - were delisted after taking legal action against the EU. Keeping Usmanov on the list could open the EU up to more legal challenges from the billionaire, which could make more of the council's classified evidence packs being made public. Confirmation that much of the evidence is spurious may have emboldened the almost 3,000 individuals and entities sanctioned by Brussels over the conflict to launch challenges of their own. Fridman also certainly believes the bloc is engaged in significant overreach. To the envoys who met on Monday, cutting Usmanov loose may have been seen as a necessary sacrifice to preserve the legitimacy of the sanctions regime. National interest The push to delist Usmanov began in Slovakia this March, when Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar argued that there were "very strong legal arguments" against the sanctioning of him and Fridman. Uzbekistan and a number of other Turkic countries - including Türkiye - reportedly lobbied Bratislava to push for his removal from the blacklist. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico is a vocal critic of EU sanctions against Russia, but Slovakia found an ally when France unexpectedly began advocating for Usmanov's delisting, citing unexplained "national security" interests. According to multiple media reports, France has been negotiating behind the scenes with Azerbaijan, where President Ilham Aliyev has apparently agreed to release two imprisoned French citizens in exchange, one of whom was jailed for spying on the country's military on behalf of French intelligence. Why did Luxembourg back off from Fridman? According to Reuters, Luxembourg backed the delisting of Fridman, who has sued the duchy for $16 billion over its freezing of his assets in 2022. Luxembourg reportedly argued that its case against Fridman would be weakened if Usmanov alone was let go, and insisted that the two billionaires be treated as a package deal. EU diplomats took to Politico to vent at the French last week, with one complaining that "if France goes ahead with this, others will come forward with their own oligarchs that should be delisted ... [then] the house of cards starts to fall." What nobody in Brussels will admit on the record is that if Usmanov is un-sanctioned, politicians and publishers across Europe will likely breathe a sigh of relief that their media outlets - many of them government-funded - will not be dragged into a legal showdown that could result in massive payouts and the collapse of the sanctions system itself. What does Usmanov's case tell us about the EU? The case exposes cracks in the EU's "united front" for Ukraine, as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put it during her State of the Union speech last week. As France and Luxembourg demonstrated, no EU member is above breaking ranks when their national interest is at stake, and the EU is sometimes capable of putting its own members' needs above Ukraine's. Is the Kiev tail wagging the EU dog? Kiev remains incandescent at the thought of its EU masters going off-script. "How can anyone seriously discuss sanctions delisting while Russia's war continues?" Vladimir Zelensky's sanctions adviser, Vladislav Vlasiuk, complained on Monday. "Usmanov and Fridman were listed because they are part of Russia's aggressive regime waging a war of aggression against Ukraine," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sybiga wrote on social media. "Delisting is unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase." What does this tell us about the EU's info-culture? No matter how unsavory a character Brussels finds him, Usmanov's string of legal victories against Western Europe's most prestigious news outlets - seen in Moscow as paranoid pillars in an increasingly hysterical echo-chamber - sends an important signal to the EU: As long as it believes what it tells itself about Russia and Russians, the legal ground it stands on is incredibly shaky. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/the-reas.text: The reason why the visit of the United States Congress to Romania was canceled last minute The delegation’s program also included a meeting with interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan. The government explains the reason for the cancellation of the visit The executive made the clarifications after several journalists requested information on the reasons why the visit of the US Congressional delegation was canceled. According to the Government, the decision is not related to the political or diplomatic agenda, but to a technical issue. „Given that there were several questions regarding the reason for the cancellation of the visit of the US Congressional delegation, we would like to clarify that this was determined by a technical problem with the aircraft on which the delegation was to travel to Romania,” the Government announced. The executive had previously announced that the visit would not take place during the day, citing „objective reasons”, without initially providing other details. A meeting was scheduled with Ilie Bolojan The American delegation was scheduled to have several meetings in Romania, including a meeting with interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan. The visit will be rescheduled. The cancellation concerns the program set for Friday, with the Government indicating that the visit would be rescheduled. The executive stated that it will return with information when a new date is set for the US Congressional delegation’s visit to Romania. From the information officially communicated so far, it does not appear that the visit has been definitively canceled. Read more: • Romania has the EU’s largest quarterly deficit: 9.2% of GDP.
